doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: Coltrane tells Ali to go to New York
summary: At the Showboat Coltrane refused Ali a sit-in but advised him to move; Ali arrived and worked with Ayler and Don Cherry.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And eventually, did people tell you, you have to go to New York? Or did you just sort of sense that that was where —

Well I mean that’s where it was. Because I used to go to New York all the time. You know I would just get in the car and drive there. And catch a bus and go there. And I knew a lot of musicians in New York. But actually I had — one night John Coltrane was playing at this club in Philly called The Showboat, it was on Lombard Street, down your way. 15th and Lombard. And I was there and I was a pretty experienced drummer at that time. And I was bugging him to let me sit in and play with him, although Elvin was kicking down doors and stuff, but I still had enough heart to ask to sit in you know. But he wouldn’t let me, because he had just started the band. This was in the early sixties, when he had just put this band together, with Elvin and McCoy, who was a real good friend of mine because we used to play a lot. And Reggie Workman, who also was — I mean he had my real good friends in the band, you know? And that’s why I felt like I needed to get this gig. But he had this guy from Detroit, who was Elvin Jones. And so I was asking him to let me sit in and I was being stupid about it. And he was telling me no, no, you know. “I just put this band together” he’d say, but he’d say, “but you know you should go to New York, man,” he’d say, “because it seems like you kind of burnt Philly up. And you should go there because there’s a lot of musicians there that are thinking like you are. More or less than here in Philly.” And so he sort of told me that and six months later I’m moving to New York actually.
And how were you thinking? He said they were thinking like you were.

Yeah well he was thinking about trying to play something other than four-four times. Trying to stretch the beat out. Trying to play a little more open and a little more freer. Because that’s what they were doing, and that’s why I felt like I could sit in and play with them. And he just said like there’s people, and he was right, because as soon as I moved to New York, the first night that I got there, Sunny Murray, which is a friend of mine also from Philly who plays drums and he was working with Albert Ayler at the time, I sat in and played with Albert Ayler the night that I came there, right away. And then two weeks later I got a job with Don Cherry and Pharoah Sanders had just moved to New York about the same week I did and we both got a gig with Don Cherry which lasted for about four or five months at this club, at this little coffee shop over on Sullivan Street in New York. So I immediately started working when I got to New York and with Archie Schepp and all these guys who were thinking more like I was thinking. So you know it worked out really good for me. I mean as soon as I got here I got real busy.
